post.caption: Kimberley's name began with a complaint. Diamonds found in 1871 drew diggers to a camp called New Rush. Britain's Lord Kimberley found that name undignified. Reportedly, he could neither spell nor pronounce the farm's name, Vooruitzigt. So in 1873, a proclamation named the camp the town of Kimberley. The rich blue ground of its mine became known as kimberlite. Western Australia's Kimberley region is named for the same earl. In 1979, diamonds turned up there, in a pipe at Argyle. Argyle's rock is lamproite, a cousin of kimberlite. Argyle produced about 865 million carats of rough diamonds. Photo: James St. John, CC BY 2.0.
